title: Clostridioides difficile: who to test, how to treat, and the recurrence

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the 2021 IDSA/SHEA Clostridioides difficile guideline update. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: Testing for C. difficile is appropriate after at least how many unformed stools in 24 hours, in a patient not on laxatives?
questions.why: Testing formed stool or a patient on laxatives detects colonisation, which is common and is not treated. Laboratories increasingly reject formed samples.

questions.q: After treatment, should a stool test be repeated to confirm cure?
questions.a: No; the test stays positive for weeks after recovery
d: Yes, if the patient works in healthcare
questions.why: Cure is clinical. A repeat test within a week of a positive is also discouraged, since it rarely changes management.

questions.q: What is the preferred treatment for an initial, non-fulminant episode?
questions.why: Oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily is the acceptable alternative. Metronidazole is used only if neither is available, and only for non-severe disease. Intravenous vancomycin does not reach the colon.

questions.q: Which findings define a severe episode?
a: White cell count of 15,000 or more
d: More than ten stools a day
questions.why: Fulminant disease is hypotension, ileus or megacolon. Severity changes the drug in the fulminant case, and the urgency of surgical review.

questions.q: What is the treatment of fulminant C. difficile with ileus?
questions.a: High-dose oral and rectal vancomycin, intravenous metronidazole, and surgical review
questions.why: Oral vancomycin 500 mg four times daily; the rectal route is for when the ileus stops it reaching the colon. Subtotal colectomy or a diverting loop ileostomy can be life-saving.

questions.q: A first recurrence after a course of vancomycin. Which regimen is recommended?
questions.a: Fidaxomicin, standard or extended-pulsed, or a tapered and pulsed vancomycin course
d: The same 10 days of vancomycin again
questions.why: Bezlotoxumab, a monoclonal antibody against toxin B, can be added to reduce further recurrence, with caution in heart failure.

questions.q: After multiple recurrences despite appropriate antibiotics, what is recommended?
questions.why: It succeeds in most patients with recurrent disease. Probiotics are not recommended for prevention or treatment.

questions.q: Which hand hygiene method removes C. difficile spores?
questions.why: Alcohol does not kill spores. Contact precautions, gloves and gowns, and bleach-based cleaning of the room are the other measures.

questions.q: Which antibiotics carry the highest risk of causing C. difficile infection?
questions.why: Any antibiotic can, and the risk persists for weeks after the course. Stopping the inciting antibiotic, when possible, is part of the treatment.

questions.q: A patient with C. difficile diarrhoea asks for loperamide. What is the answer?
questions.a: Avoid antimotility drugs until the infection is treated
d: Yes, once the fever has settled
questions.why: Slowing the gut in active infection has been associated with megacolon. Fluids and electrolyte replacement are the supportive care.

questions.q: Which acid-suppressing drug class is associated with C. difficile infection and is reviewed at diagnosis?
questions.why: Stopping an unnecessary proton pump inhibitor is reasonable; stopping a necessary one is not. The association is modest but consistent.

questions.q: A formed-stool sample from an asymptomatic patient is positive on a screening test. What is done?
questions.a: Nothing; asymptomatic carriage is not treated
questions.why: Carriage is common in hospitals and treatment does not clear it durably. The test should not have been sent.
